question: Under Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c), a seller or seller's agent has no duty to disclose or release information about:
choice_a: Whether a death by natural causes, suicide, or accident unrelated to the property's condition occurred on the property, or whether a previous occupant had, has, or may have had AIDS, HIV-related illness, or HIV infection
choice_c: Known defects in the plumbing system
choice_d: Whether the property lies within a floodplain
explanation: Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) creates a specific carve-out relieving sellers and their agents of any duty to disclose deaths on the property (other than those related to the property's physical condition) or a prior occupant's AIDS/HIV status -- a stigmatized-property protection distinct from the general duty to disclose known physical defects.
source_note: Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) (Seller Disclosure Requirements -- stigmatized property/HIV exemption), verified via texas.public.law and codes.findlaw.com

question: Among the statutory exemptions in Texas Property Code Section 5.008(e) from the requirement to provide a Seller's Disclosure Notice is a sale of:
choice_a: A new residence that has never been occupied
choice_c: Any home located within a floodplain
choice_d: Any home sold through a licensed broker
explanation: Section 5.008(e) lists roughly a dozen exempt transfer categories, including new, previously unoccupied residences, foreclosure and bankruptcy transfers, transfers between co-owners or certain family members, divorce-related transfers, and transfers where a dwelling's value does not exceed 5% of the property's total value -- none of which turn on the home's age, floodplain location, or use of a broker.
source_note: Texas Property Code Section 5.008(e) (Seller Disclosure Requirements -- statutory exemptions), verified via texas.public.law and codes.findlaw.com

question: Texas Property Code Section 5.008(e) exempts a transfer from the Seller's Disclosure Notice requirement where the value of any dwelling on the property does not exceed:
choice_a: Five percent of the value of the property
choice_b: Fifty percent of the value of the property
choice_c: No such value-based exemption exists under Section 5.008
choice_d: One hundred percent of the value of the property
explanation: One of the less-obvious exemptions under Section 5.008(e) applies to transfers where a dwelling's value makes up 5% or less of the total property value -- typically relevant to large rural or ranch tracts where any residential structure is incidental to the land's overall value.
source_note: Texas Property Code Section 5.008(e) (Seller Disclosure Requirements -- statutory exemptions), verified via texas.public.law and codes.findlaw.com

question: If a seller fails to deliver the required Seller's Disclosure Notice to the buyer on or before the effective date of a Texas residential contract, Property Code Section 5.008(f) gives the buyer the right to:
choice_a: Terminate the contract for any reason within seven days after actually receiving the notice
choice_c: Sue for specific performance only, with no termination right
choice_d: Automatically void the sale after closing, with no time limit on doing so
explanation: Property Code Section 5.008(f) requires delivery of the Seller's Disclosure Notice on or before the effective date of an executory contract; if delivery is delayed, the buyer gains an unconditional right to terminate for any reason within seven days after actually receiving the notice, protecting buyers who contract before seeing the disclosure.
source_note: Texas Property Code Section 5.008(f) (Seller Disclosure Requirements -- timing and termination right), verified via texas.public.law and codes.findlaw.com

question: Texas regulates mold-related work through the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation under Occupations Code Chapter 1958, which establishes separate license categories for:
choice_a: Mold assessors, who inspect and develop remediation protocols, and mold remediators, who perform the actual cleanup/removal work
choice_b: A single combined 'mold contractor' license with no distinction between inspection and cleanup roles
choice_c: Only mold remediators, leaving mold assessment entirely unregulated
choice_d: Real estate brokers, who are automatically authorized to perform mold work under their brokerage license
explanation: Occupations Code Chapter 1958 creates distinct licensing tracks for mold assessors (who inspect, sample, and develop management/remediation plans) and mold remediators (who perform the physical removal, cleaning, or treatment work) -- a bifurcated structure meant to keep the diagnosing party separate from the party performing the paid remediation.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Chapter 1958, Section 1958.001 (Mold Assessors and Remediators -- definitions), verified via texas.public.law

question: Under Texas Occupations Code Section 1958.154, after completing mold remediation work a license holder must deliver a certificate to the property owner confirming the mold contamination was remediated, and when later selling the property, the owner must:
choice_a: Provide the buyer copies of all such mold remediation certificates issued within the preceding five years
choice_b: Destroy all mold remediation records immediately after receiving them
choice_c: Never disclose that remediation occurred, regardless of buyer inquiry
choice_d: Disclose remediation only if the buyer specifically asks about an unrelated defect
explanation: Occupations Code Section 1958.154 requires a mold remediation certificate to be delivered to the property owner within 10 days of completed work, and separately requires the owner to give a buyer copies of all mold remediation certificates issued within the five years preceding the sale -- an affirmative, statute-based disclosure duty layered on top of the general Section 5.008 notice.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1958.154 (Certificate of Mold Remediation; Duty of Property Owner), verified via texas.public.law

question: Texas Occupations Code Section 1958.155 protects against conflicts of interest in mold-related work by generally prohibiting a license holder from:
choice_a: Performing both mold assessment and mold remediation on the same project, or holding an ownership interest in both the assessment and remediation entities working the same job
choice_b: Ever performing mold assessment work anywhere in Texas
choice_c: Charging any fee whatsoever for mold remediation services
choice_d: Working on residential property, as opposed to commercial property
explanation: Section 1958.155 bars the same license holder from both assessing and remediating the same mold project, and bars common ownership between the assessing and remediating entities on that project, so the assessor's diagnosis and scope-of-work findings are not tainted by a financial stake in the remediation contract that follows.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1958.155 (Independence Requirements), verified via texas.public.law

question: The federal lead-based paint disclosure rule (42 U.S.C. Section 4852d) does NOT apply to certain categories of housing, including:
choice_a: Housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities (unless a child under six resides there), zero-bedroom units, and short-term rentals of 100 days or less
choice_b: Every home built before 1978, without exception
choice_c: Only commercial property, since the rule otherwise covers all residential housing regardless of age
choice_d: Only property sold through a licensed broker
explanation: The federal lead-based paint disclosure rule carves out several exemptions even for pre-1978 housing: units without bedrooms, short-term rentals of 100 days or less, housing for the elderly or disabled (absent a resident child under six), homes already certified lead-free by an inspection, and foreclosure sales.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 4852d; EPA lead-based paint real estate disclosure rule, verified via epa.gov

question: Under the federal lead-based paint disclosure rule, a buyer of pre-1978 target housing is generally entitled to a period of how many days to conduct a lead-based paint inspection or risk assessment before becoming obligated under the contract, absent a different mutually agreed written period?
choice_d: There is no such right under federal law
explanation: 42 U.S.C. Section 4852d gives homebuyers a 10-day window (unless the parties mutually agree in writing to a different period, or the buyer knowingly waives the opportunity) to conduct a lead-based paint inspection or risk assessment before becoming contractually obligated to purchase.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 4852d (lead-based paint disclosure -- inspection opportunity), verified via law.cornell.edu

question: Sellers, landlords, and their agents must retain signed copies of federal lead-based paint disclosure documents for how long, and what type of enhanced damages can a court award a buyer for a knowing violation?
choice_a: Three years after the sale or lease begins, and up to treble (three times) the buyer's actual damages
choice_b: Ninety days, and no monetary damages of any kind are recoverable
choice_c: Indefinitely, with no monetary remedy ever available
choice_d: One year, and only nominal damages of one dollar
explanation: Sellers, landlords, and agents must keep signed lead-based paint disclosure records for three years, and 42 U.S.C. Section 4852d authorizes a court to award a buyer up to treble (three times) actual damages for a knowing violation, plus attorney's fees and costs -- a meaningfully higher stakes disclosure obligation than many other property condition items.
source_note: 42 U.S.C. Section 4852d (lead-based paint disclosure -- record retention and penalties), verified via law.cornell.edu and epa.gov

question: Regarding a registered sex offender residing near or within a property being sold, Texas real estate licensees generally:
choice_a: Have no statutory duty to investigate or disclose sex offender registry information, similar to the no-duty treatment given to other off-property or stigmatizing conditions unrelated to the property's physical condition
choice_b: Must personally check the registry and disclose findings for every listed property
choice_c: Are strictly liable for any nearby registered offender regardless of whether they knew or disclosed anything
choice_d: Must include sex offender registry printouts in every Seller's Disclosure Notice
explanation: Neither Texas Property Code Section 5.008 nor TREC rules impose an affirmative duty on sellers or licensees to research or disclose sex offender registry information -- consistent with the broader principle (paralleling the statutory HIV/death carve-out in 5.008(c)) that off-property, non-physical conditions generally fall outside the mandatory disclosure framework, though licensees may direct interested buyers to the public registry.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline VI.B (environmental and property disclosure obligations and liability -- Megan's Law/registry disclosure limits), Pearson VUE #094401; Texas Property Code Section 5.008

question: Following Hurricane Harvey, the Texas Legislature amended Property Code Section 5.008 to expand the Seller's Disclosure Notice to require more detailed disclosure of:
choice_a: The property's flood history, current flood insurance coverage, and location within a floodplain or a reservoir's flood pool
choice_b: The homeowner's personal income and credit history
choice_d: Nothing -- no flood-related amendments to Section 5.008 followed Hurricane Harvey
explanation: In response to Hurricane Harvey's widespread flooding, Texas amended the Property Code Section 5.008 disclosure form to require more specific flood-related disclosures, including previous flooding, current flood insurance coverage, and whether the property lies within a designated floodplain or a reservoir's flood pool -- a meaningful expansion beyond the notice's pre-2019 flood language.
source_note: Texas Property Code Section 5.008 (post-Hurricane Harvey flood disclosure amendments, 2019); National/General Broker Content Outline VI.A.1.e

question: A 'latent defect' that triggers a seller's or licensee's disclosure duty is best described as a defect that is:
choice_a: Hidden or not readily observable through a buyer's reasonable inspection, as opposed to a 'patent' defect that is plainly visible
choice_b: Always visible to any buyer upon a casual walk-through of the property
choice_c: Never subject to any disclosure duty under Texas or federal law
choice_d: Relevant only to commercial property transactions
explanation: A latent defect is a hidden flaw not discoverable through a buyer's reasonable inspection -- such as a concealed foundation crack or hidden plumbing leak -- which is precisely why disclosure duties focus heavily on latent defects; a patent (open and obvious) defect is generally considered something a buyer should discover on their own inspection.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline VI.B (environmental and property disclosure obligations and liability -- latent vs. patent defects), Pearson VUE #094401

question: The EPA-recommended action level at which radon mitigation is advised is 4 picocuries per liter (pCi/L) of air; unlike the federal lead-based paint disclosure rule, Texas:
choice_a: Has no state statute mandating radon testing or disclosure in residential real estate transactions
choice_b: Requires radon testing before every residential closing in the state
choice_c: Bans the installation of radon mitigation systems
choice_d: Requires radon disclosure only for commercial buildings, never residential
explanation: While the EPA recommends radon mitigation at or above 4 pCi/L and radon is a recognized environmental hazard licensees should be alert to, Texas has no state statute comparable to the federal lead-based paint law mandating radon testing or disclosure in real estate transactions -- a meaningful contrast candidates should not assume away.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline VI.A.1.b (asbestos, radon, and mold), Pearson VUE #094401

question: Asbestos abatement and removal work in Texas structures is regulated primarily to protect against the release of airborne fibers linked to respiratory disease, and such work is subject to:
choice_a: Licensing and notification/work-practice requirements under federal EPA/NESHAP rules and Texas Department of State Health Services asbestos program regulations
choice_b: No regulation whatsoever, since asbestos work is left entirely to market self-policing
choice_c: Only local municipal zoning ordinances, with no state or federal role
choice_d: Only the Texas Real Estate Commission's advertising rule
explanation: Asbestos abatement is regulated at the federal level through EPA's National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants (NESHAP) work-practice and notification rules, and at the state level through the Texas Department of State Health Services' asbestos licensing program -- a dual regulatory structure licensees should recognize when a pre-renovation inspection or demolition raises asbestos concerns.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline VI.A.1.b (asbestos, radon, and mold), Pearson VUE #094401
